summary: Italy is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorisation being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90, checked via the official Visto per l'Italia portal.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since 11 June 2024.

For stays over 90 days: work, family reunification and other long-stay purposes. Within 8 days of arrival you must apply for a residence permit (permesso di soggiorno). Confirm the fee for your category with the consulate.

fee.notes: Required for courses longer than 90 days; needs proof of enrolment, funds, accommodation and health insurance. Confirm the current fee with the consulate.

source.name: Visto per l'Italia — Italian MFA visa portal

fee.notes: For highly qualified remote workers and freelancers working for non-Italian clients; income threshold of roughly €25,000–28,000 per year plus insurance and accommodation. Confirm requirements with the consulate.

source.name: Visto per l'Italia — Italian MFA visa portal

fee.notes: Requires a work authorisation (nulla osta) obtained by the employer in Italy, usually within the annual decreto flussi quota system.

source.name: Visto per l'Italia — Italian MFA visa portal

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

source.name: Visto per l'Italia — Italian MFA visa portal

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

source.name: Visto per l'Italia — Italian MFA visa portal

proofOfFunds.text: Italy sets means of subsistence on a sliding scale by trip length (Ministry of the Interior directive of 1 March 2000): about €270 total for stays up to 5 days, then roughly €45 per day for one traveller on longer stays (less per person for couples/groups). Confirm current figures with the consulate.

source.name: Visto per l'Italia — Italian MFA visa portal

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travellers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border — there is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorisation System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travellers will need an ETIAS travel authorisation to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards are accepted almost everywhere and merchants are legally required to take them, but small bars, market stalls and some family trattorias still prefer cash — carry some euros.

safety.text: Italy is a very safe destination. The main risks for visitors are pickpocketing on public transport in Rome, Milan and Naples, and around crowded sights and train stations.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Italy Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September–October combine pleasant weather with manageable crowds; August is hot, busy on the coast, and many city businesses close for the Ferragosto holidays.

tips.text: Historic city centres are restricted traffic zones (ZTL) — driving a rental car past the camera-enforced signs in Florence, Rome or Milan triggers automatic fines that follow you home.
Most cities charge a per-night tourist tax (typically €1–10 depending on city and hotel class, e.g. up to €10 in Rome), usually paid at the accommodation and not included in booking prices.
Validate regional train and bus tickets in the platform machines before boarding — travelling with an unvalidated ticket earns an on-the-spot fine.
Apply for ETIAS only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site once it becomes mandatory — unofficial sites charge inflated fees.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Italy?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Italy and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorisation (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does an Italy Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries. Check your requirement on the official Visto per l'Italia portal.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Italy?
faq.answer: ETIAS is being phased in for visa-exempt travellers. During the transition period travellers without ETIAS are still admitted; once fully mandatory, the €20 online authorisation will be required before boarding. Check the official EU website for the current status.

faq.question: Does Italy have a digital nomad visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Since 2024 Italy issues a digital nomad visa for highly qualified remote workers earning roughly €25,000–28,000+ per year, with health insurance and accommodation requirements. Apply at the Italian consulate for your place of residence; after arrival you must request a residence permit within 8 days.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Italy without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but must register locally after 3 months.
